opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters because the real test of intelligence isn't how well you do in one environment you've been tuned for — it's whether you can walk into an unfamiliar one and still figure out what's going on.

Right now, a lot of agents are very good inside a narrow world. You train them on a particular game, a particular website, a particular codebase, and they look impressive. But change the rules a little, swap the interface, give them a new set of tools, and performance can fall off a cliff. That tells you the agent learned the world, not how to learn worlds.

Humans are different. You can drop a person into a new video game, a new job, a new country, and within a short time they've built a rough model: what are the objects here, what actions do I have, what seems to cause what, what am I actually trying to achieve. That ability to rapidly form and revise a model of an environment is, to me, much closer to the core of general intelligence than any single benchmark score.

There's also a very practical reason. The world we want agents to operate in isn't one world, it's thousands of them. Every company's software stack is its own little universe. Every user's computer is set up differently. Physical environments vary endlessly. If each new setting requires collecting fresh data and retraining, agents will never scale. But if an agent can transfer what it knows, about exploration, about tool use, about recovering from mistakes, then each new world becomes cheap to enter.

And I'd add one more thing: training across many diverse worlds is probably also how you get there. When an agent is forced to succeed across lots of environments with different dynamics, it can't just memorize shortcuts. It has to discover more abstract, reusable strategies. So diversity of worlds isn't only the goal; it's also the curriculum. That's why I find this direction so exciting.

r001.rationale: It says agents should handle unfamiliar environments and transfer what they know across varied settings, supporting generalization beyond a single trained world.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention embodied robotics or predict that robotics and large AI models will ultimately converge completely.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it matters because the real test of intelligence isn't how well you do in one environment, it's how well you adapt when the environment changes. A lot of agents today look impressive inside the world they were trained in, but the moment you drop them into a different interface, a different set of rules, a different physics, they fall apart. That tells you they've memorized a world rather than learned how to understand one.

Humans don't work that way. If you learn to drive a car, you can get into a different car and figure it out. If you pick up a new video game, you don't start from zero, you bring everything you know about goals, obstacles, cause and effect. That transfer is the thing we actually care about.

So when we push agents to operate across many worlds, we're forcing them to build representations that are general rather than brittle. Each new world is a kind of stress test: it exposes which parts of the agent's knowledge are real understanding and which parts are shortcuts that only happened to work before.

And practically, the real world is not one world. It's a huge collection of environments that look nothing like each other, from a browser to a robot arm to a conversation with a person. If we want agents to be useful out there, they have to be comfortable walking into a place they've never seen and acting sensibly. That's why I think cross-world capability isn't a side feature, it's close to the core of what it means to build a capable agent.

r001.rationale: The response says operating across many worlds forces agents to build general rather than brittle representations, helping them act sensibly across the varied environments of the real world.

r002.rationale: The response mentions robot arms as one real-world environment, but does not predict that embodied robotics and large AI models will ultimately converge completely.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters because an agent can look very capable in one environment while depending heavily on the rules of that environment. When the tools, feedback, or constraints change, you find out whether it has learned something transferable or just learned how to succeed in one setting.

Operating across different worlds pushes an agent to do two things together: carry useful knowledge forward and recognize when its assumptions no longer apply. It has to explore, learn from feedback, and adjust its behavior.

That matters for practical use because even everyday tasks involve moving between environments—different applications, different people, different expectations. We want an agent that can handle those transitions, recognize what it doesn’t understand, and ask for help when it needs to.

r001.rationale: The response connects operating across different worlds with transferable learning and handling transitions among everyday environments, clearly conveying improved generalization across settings in our world.

r002.rationale: The response makes no prediction about embodied robotics and large AI models converging.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it matters because an agent can look very capable in one environment while actually depending on a lot of assumptions built into that environment. Change the tools, the rules, or the way information is presented, and its performance can fall apart.

Operating across different worlds pushes an agent to learn what transfers: how to explore, understand constraints, plan, and recover when something goes wrong. It also has to recognize what doesn’t transfer and learn the new rules instead of blindly applying an old strategy.

That’s important because the real world keeps changing. We want agents that can adapt to unfamiliar situations, recognize uncertainty, and ask for help when they need it. Success in one world is useful, but adapting across worlds gives us stronger evidence of a more general capability.

r001.rationale: The response says cross-world adaptation provides stronger evidence of general capability and helps agents adapt to changing real-world situations, but it does not clearly state that this improves generalization within our world.

r002.rationale: The response makes no prediction about embodied robotics and large AI models converging completely.
